Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

items.title: Deletion of Furin Facilitates Efficient and Versatile Coronavirus Pseudotyped Particle Generation
items.blurb: Coronaviruses bring threats to both humans and animals. To initiate successful infections, coronaviruses must first navigate entry into a host cell. Coronavirus spike-bearing pseudotyped particle systems are indispensable tools for studying coronavirus entry and evaluating neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors. However, pseudotyped particle titers can be low when packaged particles bear coronavirus spikes that contain the furin cleavage site, and this has been a limitation for pseudotyped particle production and applications. Here, we demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of furin protease in HEK293T cells significantly enhances the production of functional pseudotyped particles bearing spikes containing the furin cleavage site, including those from SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and MHV-JHM. Moreover, deletion of endogenous furin in producer cells yields an effect equivalent to deletion of the furin cleavage site, but with broader application across different spike proteins, and without virus manipulation. This work establishes a simple and effective platform to improve coronavirus pseudotyped particle systems by eliminating furin-mediated pre-activation, enabling more efficient and reliable production for downstream applications.

items.title: A Novel Autoantibody against LAG-3 in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
items.blurb: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease characterized by immune tolerance loss, although its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Immune checkpoint molecules maintain peripheral tolerance, and their dysregulation contributes to autoimmunity. Autoantibodies against lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG-3), an immune checkpoint molecule, were identified in a subset of patients with SLE. We enrolled 130 patients with SLE, 119 patients with other autoimmune diseases, and 32 healthy controls. The sera of patients with SLE were screened for antibodies against various immune checkpoint molecules to identify clinically relevant disease-specific autoantibodies against LAG-3. Functional assays were performed to assess the effect of anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies on the interaction between LAG-3 and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II. Pathogenic relevance was evaluated using genetic deletion and immunization-based mouse models. Anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies were detected in 52/130 patients with SLE (40.0%) but only 4 of 119 patients with other autoimmune diseases (3.4%). These autoantibodies were associated with lupus nephritis and higher disease activity. In mice, Lag3 deletion or human LAG-3 immunization induced lupus-like autoimmunity. These findings support the clinical relevance of anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies in SLE and implicate LAG-3 checkpoint disruption in lupus-like autoimmunity.

items.title: Spatial metabolic ecosystems shape the architecture of IDH-mutant glioma
items.blurb: The principles governing tissue organization in IDH-mutant glioma remain poorly understood, particularly in the absence of hypoxia and necrosis that define IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Here, we integrated spatial transcriptomics, metabolomics and histology across co-registered serial tissue sections, generating a multidimensional atlas of IDH-mutant glioma. Integration with an independent spatial transcriptomics cohort and a single cell atlas (n=101 samples), enabled resolution of metabolic and cellular heterogeneity underlying tissue organization. We identified twelve conserved spatial niches with distinct metabolic identities that could not be explained by cellular composition or histology alone. Beyond these ecosystems, we discovered a transcriptionally and epigenetically intermediate malignant cell state enriched in WHO grade 2/3 oligodendroglioma, and spatially segregated myeloid programs. Importantly, progression following chemoradiotherapy was associated with expansion of a glutathione-rich, NRF2-associated antioxidant niche. Together, our findings establish metabolic specialization as a fundamental dimension of glioma organization, providing new insight into tumor heterogeneity, progression and treatment-associated adaptation.

In the moments after the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 semi-final victory over the Utah Royals last weekend, all of Audi Field was in rapture. In the stands, around 20,000 Spirit supporters had filled the stadium to capacity, the sixth time they’d done so in 2026. They filled the place with the type of wondrous noise that’s become alien in DC sports in recent years, the type of gleeful adoration reserved for the city’s rare winners. The Spirit will return to their home stadium to face the Kansas City Current in the NWSL championship this Saturday.

In short order, the Spirit’s players made their way to the north end of the stadium, taking their celebrations into the crowd with their supporters. Perhaps no player has done more to push the Spirit into not only local but national relevance than US women’s national team forward Trinity Rodman, and Rodman herself grabbed a flag from a fan, jubilantly waving it above the crowd. items.title: DR Congo: Evaluation conjointe des besoins en matière d’Education et Protection RDC-2026
items.blurb:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Education Cluster, Save the Children, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Le rapport de l’évaluation conjointe des besoins d’Education et de Protection menée en collaboration avec le secteur de la Protection met en évidence les résultats suivants :

  • Taux d’abandon de 12,5 % au cours de l’année scolaire 2025-2026, principalement lié aux difficultés socio-économiques des ménages, aux déplacements forcés, aux travaux domestiques, ainsi qu’aux mariages et grossesses précoces.
  • 131 établissements sur 266 (50 %) rapportent des absences scolaires liées à la gestion des menstruations.
  • 76 responsables d’établissements sur 266 (28%) affirment que les établissements ont subi des pillages ou vols perpétrés par des groupes armés depuis le début de l’année 2026, tandis que 47 sur 266 (18%) ont relevé l’occupation de salles de classe par des forces ou groupes armés.
  • L’inclusion des enfants en situation de handicap demeure limitée, avec peu de mesures spécifiques favorisant leur participation et leur maintien à l’école.
  • Seuls 51 établissements sur 266 (19 %) disposent d’un accès à l’eau potable provenant de leur principale source d’approvisionnement.
  • 114 établissements (43 %) ne disposent pas de latrines séparées pour les filles et les garçons.
  • 101 établissements sur 266 (38 %) signalent la présence d’enfants présentant des signes de détresse psychosociale, notamment des cauchemars, une tristesse persistante, une anxiété élevée, de la fatigue extrême, des comportements violents ou de l’isolement.
  • Seuls 70 établissements sur 266 (26%) disposent d’un mécanisme de référencement VBG adapté aux enfants et permettant l’orientation vers des services spécialisés.

Malgré ces défis, les consultations avec les enfants montrent que l’école reste perçue comme un espace de protection, de stabilité et d’espoir. Comme l’a souligné un enfant de 8 à 11 ans : « A l’école, on étudie et on oublie la guerre. »

items.title: oPt: Gaza Strip | Learning Spaces Assessment Report (November 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Education Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

The assessment covered 962 learning spaces across Gaza’s five governorates between 21 May and 12 August 2026, reporting 581,111 enrolments and 15,709 teachers. In the absence of permanent education infrastructure, Temporary learning spaces, community-led initiatives and private learning spaces have sustained education despite severe disruption. Most learning spaces reported being fully functional and using learning content consistent with that of the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE). These responses provide limited information about instructional time, safety, inclusion or the resources available to learners.

The assessment identified substantial pressure on the learning spaces. A ten-point checklist classified 362 as good, 494 as at risk and 106 as critical. At-risk spaces remain operational but need improvements to support children’s safety, wellbeing and learning. Critical spaces are partly operating, temporarily closed or missing several basic facilities and services. These categories guide support priorities; they do not assess building safety. Limited covered space and widespread double or triple shifts constrain provision. Multiple shifts expand access but may reduce teaching time and increase pressure on facilities. Nearly half of assessed spaces reported additional demand from displaced children or waiting lists.

Protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and basic services remain uneven. Children face barriers linked to insecurity, distance, transport, psychological distress and household responsibilities. Protection referral mechanisms and disaster preparedness measures are not consistently available, particularly in community-led initiatives. Gaps in safe drinking water, appropriate sanitation, electricity and first-aid capacity affect children’s safety, dignity and participation.

Disability inclusion requires attention. Although children with disabilities were enrolled across many spaces, accessible facilities, inclusive sanitation and adapted learning materials were less widely available. Enrolment alone does not demonstrate meaningful participation. Accessibility, adapted materials, assistive products, transport and specialist referrals need to be integrated into programme planning and budgets.

Most learning spaces reported using clearly defined learning content. Shortages of furniture and educational materials constrained teaching. Training and psychosocial support for teachers were uneven, particularly in community-led initiatives, where reliance on volunteers also raises concerns about staff retention and continuity. Community participation provides a foundation for local accountability, although women’s and learners’ representation needs strengthening.

The assessment provides a common evidence base for the Cluster’s 2027 planning, advocacy and resource mobilisation to sustain access, improve learning conditions and support pathways to recognised formal education. Its central finding is that sustaining enrolment requires conditions that enable children to attend regularly, participate meaningfully and learn. The findings describe assessed learning spaces and will be considered alongside other evidence on learning outcomes and children’s wider education needs across Gaza. Section 1.1 sets out the priorities for collective action.

What does this mean for the response

items.title: India's Hidden Natural Wonders: 9 Geological Sites Seeking UNESCO World Heritage Recognition
items.blurb: India's most extraordinary landscapes do not always announce themselves with grand monuments or marked tourist trails. Some are hidden beneath tropical forests, others rise out of the sea, and a few preserve evidence of geological events that unfolded millions of years ago. Now, several of these remarkable places are attracting international attention. India's UNESCO Tentative List has expanded in 2026, with two particularly fascinating natural heritage additions in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands: the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang and the Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, comprising Barren and Narcondam islands. These additions build on seven natural heritage properties submitted in August 2025, taking the story beyond a handful of destinations to a remarkable cross-section of India's geological history. But what makes these places special, where can travellers experience them, and what should visitors know before setting out? More importantly, how can we explore them without damaging the very landscapes that make them extraordinary? A landscape shaped by two kinds of volcanoes The first of the two new natural properties is the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang, on Great Andaman Island, about 100 km north of Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair). Baratang's Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex, Andaman and Nicobar Islands: Beneath Baratang's tropical canopy, ancient limestone caves and bubbling mud volcanoes reveal Earth's restless underground world. Photograph: ( Nicobar Times ) Picture a forested island where the ground opens into limestone caves, narrow fissures, and underground chambers. Over millions of years, marine organisms, including shells and corals, accumulated and compacted to form the limestone. Rainwater gradually dissolved parts of this rock, creating the intricate cave systems found here. But the island has another geological surprise. Its mud volcanoes, locally called Jalki , release slurries of mud, water, and gases rather than molten rock. Unlike conventional volcanoes, these formations do not erupt magma. They are driven by pressure and movement within underground sediment layers. After remaining dormant for around 20 years, Baratang's mud volcanoes became active again in 2025. The Geological Survey of India identified the mud volcano as a Geo-Heritage Site that year. The caves also support specialised subterranean ecosystems, making their conservation important beyond their geological appeal. The second property, Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, brings together Barren Island and Narcondam Island. Both emerged from the tectonic processes associated with the Indian Plate moving beneath the Burma microplate. Barren Island, approximately 138 km northeast of Sri Vijaya Puram, is South Asia's only active volcano. Its first recorded eruption dates to 1787. More recently, it recorded mild eruptions in September 2025, followed by an ash plume rising approximately 1.2 km in January 2026. Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, Narcondam Island: Cloaked in dense forests, Narcondam shelters rare wildlife, including its remarkable endemic hornbill, far from bustling tourist trails. Photograph: ( Andaman Ferry Ticket ) Narcondam, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Its densely forested volcanic landscape rises 710 metres above sea level and supports species found nowhere else, including the Narcondam hornbill. Unlike Barren Island, which is known for its surrounding marine environment, Narcondam is not open to tourism. Access is restricted, and visitors should not attempt independent trips or landings. These islands are important precisely because their ecosystems remain relatively undisturbed. A UNESCO listing should not be mistaken for an invitation to explore every part of them. Seven more landscapes that tell India's geological story The two Andaman additions join seven natural properties submitted to UNESCO in August 2025. Together, they reveal just how varied India's geological heritage is. In Maharashtra, the Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar preserve evidence of enormous volcanic eruptions around 66 million years ago. Their successive lava flows created the distinctive stepped rock formations of the region. Visitors should stick to established viewpoints and avoid disturbing exposed geological formations. Deccan Traps, Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, Maharashtra: Layer upon layer of ancient lava tells the story of volcanic eruptions that reshaped India's western landscape. Photograph: ( IUGS ) Off Karnataka's Malpe coast, the St Mary's Island Cluster is famous for its unusual columnar basalt formations. These polygonal rock structures developed as molten lava cooled and contracted approximately 85 million years ago. The islands are accessible by ferry, subject to seasonal conditions. Resist the temptation to collect rock fragments or climb fragile formations. Meghalaya's Meghalayan Age Caves include Mawmluh, Mawsmai, Arwah and Krem Puri. Mawmluh Cave is particularly significant because a mineral deposit found there helped establish the Meghalayan Age, the youngest stage of the Holocene geological epoch. Cave formations take thousands of years to develop, so visitors should never touch, scratch or break them. Explore with authorised guides. Nagaland's Naga Hill Ophiolite in Kiphire district offers a glimpse into the Earth's ancient oceanic crust and upper mantle. Ophiolites are fragments of ocean floor pushed onto land through tectonic activity. The landscape also has ecological significance, making local guidance and respect for wildlife essential. In Andhra Pradesh, Erra Matti Dibbalu, or the Red Sand Hills, near Visakhapatnam, displays striking red and brown sedimentary formations. Wind and water erosion have shaped these hills over time, preserving evidence of changing environmental and climatic conditions. Visitors should avoid walking over unstable formations or leaving waste behind. Further south, the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills includes the Eparchaean Unconformity and the Silathoranam natural rock arch. The latter is particularly fascinating: its formation represents an exceptionally old geological history, with the rocks in the region recording more than a billion years of Earth's past. The surrounding hills also carry religious significance, so visitors must respect temple and forest regulations. Varkala Cliffs, Kerala: Sedimentary layers meet the Arabian Sea at Varkala, where dramatic cliffs reveal millions of years of geological history. Photograph: ( Travelladda ) Finally, Kerala's Varkala Cliffs expose layers of the Warkalli Formation, dating to the Mio-Pliocene period. Their striking sedimentary bands overlook the Arabian Sea, while natural springs add to their geological importance. However, the cliffs face pressure from increasing tourism and construction. Visitors should keep away from unstable edges and follow safety instructions. The responsibility that comes with discovery A place becoming popular can bring income to nearby communities, but it can also put pressure on fragile ecosystems. The challenge is to ensure that tourism does not destroy what makes these destinations worth visiting. Before travelling, check local entry permissions, seasonal restrictions, and forest department guidelines. Some locations, particularly caves and protected islands, have restricted access. Never assume that a place being on UNESCO's Tentative List means it is open to unrestricted tourism. India's natural wonders are more than breathtaking landscapes; they are living archives of Earth's history, deserving protection for generations. Photograph: ( Travel and Leisure Asia ) Choose local guides and community-run stays wherever possible. Carry reusable water bottles, avoid single-use plastics, and take all waste back with you. Do not collect rocks, fossils, shells or other natural material. At coastal destinations, avoid disturbing marine habitats, and at forest sites, keep noise levels low and maintain a safe distance from wildlife. There are already examples of tourism supporting conservation across India. In Nagaland's Khonoma village , community-led tourism allows visitors to experience local culture while supporting conservation efforts. Similarly, community-led travel companies are creating opportunities for travellers to contribute directly to local livelihoods. Travellers can also take inspiration from five Indian journeys that support wildlife and nature conservation and learn from sustainable travel practices that minimise waste and respect local ecosystems. India's geological heritage is not simply a collection of spectacular views. These landscapes preserve evidence of volcanic eruptions, shifting tectonic plates, ancient oceans and evolving ecosystems. Their importance extends far beyond their potential as tourist destinations. Being included on UNESCO's Tentative List is an important step towards international recognition, but it is not the finish line. The real achievement will be ensuring that these places remain intact for generations to come. After all, the best way to experience a natural wonder is to leave it just as wonderful for the next person. Sources ' Seven Natural Heritage Sites from India Added to UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage ': by Ministry of Culture for Press Information Bureau, Published on 18 September 2025. ' Sustainable Tourism: Travel with Purpose ': by Meghalaya Tourism, official tourism website, undated

items.title: A Home That Lets Nature Take Centre Stage: Inside a Yercaud House Built Around a Tree
items.blurb: Imagine walking into a house and finding a stream flowing beneath your feet. Not outside the entrance or in a garden designed to resemble a natural waterbody, but directly beneath a transparent glass floor. Look up, and there is a tree framed by glass walls and a glass roof. Walk a little further, and the architecture opens towards a valley, allowing the surrounding landscape to become part of the experience. This is Whispers of the Wild, a residential project by MAWI Design, led by Chennai-based architect Malli Saravanan , in Yercaud, Tamil Nadu. But the most interesting thing about this house is not what its architects added to the landscape. It is what they chose not to take away. Spread across a 10,000-square-foot plot in the eco-sensitive Shervaroy Hills, the 2,400-square-foot residence was designed for a family of six. Completed in 2024, it occupies two levels and sits within Wild Orchid, a 100-acre residential community that follows an eco-sensitive development approach. “We wanted the terrain to flow naturally over here and then bring the entire thing out,” Saravanan tells The Better India . “I wanted much of it to remain tucked into the landscape, with its built form designed to sit beneath the surrounding tree canopy.” The tree that became the centre of the design When the MAWI Design team first visited the property, they found a sloping site with a valley opening up on one side. A mature tree occupied a prominent position on the land, its canopy extending across the site. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. The team first conducted a total-station survey and mapped the trees across the property. This helped them understand where the existing vegetation stood and how the proposed structure could be positioned without cutting them down. “We made sure that we didn't want to cut any of the trees, and we tried to work around them without cutting the tree,” Saravanan explains. The design was subsequently broken into three architectural fragments, allowing the tree to remain at the centre of the composition. “As visitors enter the house, their first visual connection is with this tree. The private and communal spaces open towards an L-shaped deck that wraps around it, creating a shared outdoor space overlooking the valley.” “The tree is not retained as a decorative feature. We tried to retain this tree as the hero of the site and started building a story around this tree,” he says. The same idea extends to the interiors. Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement , while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. The master bedroom, meanwhile, projects outwards in a cantilevered form. Its glass frame opens towards a panoramic view of the valley. Saravanan points out that the corners have been kept free of columns to preserve the expansive views. “We don't have any TV walls and stuff, so the bedrooms are designed to open towards nature, too,” he says, describing the decision to make the surrounding landscape the primary visual experience. A stream that disappeared, and an attempt to bring back its memory One of the most distinctive features of Whispers of the Wild is its entrance foyer. Here, the team separated two building blocks to create a transition space that feels open rather than enclosed. They also introduced a cascading water feature beneath a glass floor. There is a story behind this intervention. The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement, while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors. Photograph: (mawidesign.india) “We tried to pull out the rocks that were there at the site. And then we set up a water feature so that when one comes into this foyer space, the flooring is completely glass, so the water will be flowing underneath,” Saravanan says. The experience is deliberately immersive. The glass floor reveals the water below, while glass on the opposite side reflects the trees. A glass roof completes the visual connection with the surroundings. What happens during heavy rainfall? The team incorporated rainwater harvesting and constructed a storage tank to collect water from the roof and other catchment areas for use within the house. “Since it is a slope side, we have made sure that when there is heavy rain, the water gets collected and then it is harvested inside the ground, and the overflow gets down to the valley,” Saravanan says. There is, however, an important distinction in the project's assessment of water systems. Saravanan confirms that the team conducted a soil test and a general site survey, but did not undertake a separate hydrological assessment . What happens when the house borrows from the landscape? The walls of the house incorporate locally available random rubble stones, many sourced from within the property or nearby areas. Saravanan explains that construction activity in and around Yercaud often brings up large boulders when soil is excavated. Some of these were already available on the property, while smaller stones were sourced from nearby community areas. “We use this material as a kind of expression of the context. We use the same material in the exterior and also in the interior, so that we create a very timeless kind of palette inside the house,” he says. The rubble stone is used as an exterior-facing element over brick construction, rather than as the primary structural wall. According to Saravanan, the thickness and overall mass of the wall contribute to thermal comfort within the house. The flooring uses leathered Kota stone. Saravanan wanted the sensation of walking indoors to resemble the experience of walking outdoors. The stone's natural texture and coolness were important considerations. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) “For us, the first thing is experiential. The second is the sustainable aspect of it, and third is the aesthetics,” he explains. Oxide finishes and other natural materials complete the palette. The intention was not to create a polished, artificial version of nature, but to let the materials sit comfortably within the surrounding landscape. The team also retained the site's existing vegetation, including fruit-bearing plants and a fig tree. Saravanan says they avoided introducing non-native plants. The one notable addition was bamboo, planted along the property boundary. It serves two purposes. The community has a pathway running along the edge of the property, and the bamboo provides visual privacy for the residents . It also contributes to the sensory experience of the house. “We love the rustling sounds. So whenever there is wind, you listen to the rustling sounds, and it adds to the overall experience of the space,” he says. Does wildlife find a place here, too? A house in a hillside landscape cannot be understood only through its architecture. The Shervaroy Hills have their own distinctive vegetation, including shrubs and fruit-bearing plants. Saravanan says the team tried to retain the existing flora and make the new landscape blend with the region. He has also noticed changes in the presence of birds and other smaller wildlife around the property. “Butterflies, birds, and peacocks started coming after this,” he says, adding that peacocks are frequently seen around the house. A home that changes how its residents experience nature Interestingly, Whispers of the Wild was not originally conceived as a permanent retirement home. The client, 67-year-old Chandrapratapan from Salem, purchased the property. “One of our favourite things about living here is never knowing what we might see in the morning. Peacocks often wander by in the garden, squirrels move between the trees, and occasionally we spot a mongoose passing through. We've started recognising different birds by their calls. The old tree is probably the busiest spot on the property, with birds and insects constantly moving through it,” he shares with The Better India . “This has made us much more aware of all the life we share this place with. We love that we've been able to preserve much of what was already here — the trees, the slope and the natural landscape,” Chandrapratap adds. Saravanan also believes this reflects a shift in how people think about their homes. “We are in a very rushed world, with all these tensions and pressure, running here and there. At the end of it, people want to spend time for themselves,” he says. He has noticed more people looking beyond metropolitan neighbourhoods for homes that offer a connection with nature and a sense of calm. For him, this is not simply about having a second home or spending money on elaborate interiors. It is about the relationship between people, their surroundings and the communities they live in. Can building with nature also make financial sense? There is another question worth asking. Is this approach financially viable, or is it an architectural luxury accessible only to people who can afford expensive homes in the hills? Saravanan puts the construction cost of Whispers of the Wild at approximately Rs 1.3-1.4 crore. He considers this reasonable for a project of its scale and location, particularly because transporting materials to a hill station and arranging labour can increase construction costs. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mawi Design (@mawidesign.india) “We had all those good elements around the site. We wanted the site not to be manicured. We wanted things to be imperfect and just flow seamlessly,” he says. “We don't know where that new landscape starts or where the new construction starts. It should feel like it's very well lived in, especially the exterior parts.” The project does not establish that this approach is cheaper in every situation. Its costs depend on the terrain, construction requirements, materials and site conditions. But it offers an example of how existing natural features can become part of the architectural experience rather than being removed and recreated. Before building on a hillside, what should architects reconsider? For Saravanan, the first step is to understand the site before drawing up the building. “First, we need to understand the existing terrain, the flora, the fauna, and the existing site conditions. Making less impact on nature is the first fundamental thing they need to consider,” he says. He believes the value of a mature tree, for instance, cannot be measured simply in terms of the money required to plant another one. “Today, we can buy anything, but a well-grown tree like this, with whatever money they want, they can't buy it.” He also emphasises the importance of keeping the building footprint small. At Whispers of the Wild, the architects used cantilevered sections and elevated portions to reduce the amount of building mass touching the ground. The intention was to allow the landscape to continue around the structure. “If the footprint is very small, it is always better. It is the idea that a building does not always need to begin with a cleared, levelled piece of land,” he adds. All pictures: mawidesign.india

items.title: Promise Me, America by Joe Biden review – former president defends his decisions

New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle

Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party.

Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election.
